extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literary criticism, narrative theory, and creative writers interested in Booth's methodology
extracted.subtask_description: A compact methodology for reading, critiquing, and constructing fiction that foregrounds the rhetorical relations among author, implied author, narrator, text, and reader and emphasizes ethical and pluralistic judgement. Useful for close readers, literary critics, and writers evaluating narrative choices such as voice, distance, and moral guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refuting dogmatic critical methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics should resist stolid doctrines that impose abstract rules about what novelists do; instead analyze how good novelists actually create meanings and effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Booth spends several chapters refuting critical dogmas (purity, realism, overemphasis on language or reader-response) and recommends a methodology that examines what authors actually do rather than applying blanket 'True' or 'Pure' standards. Watch for modern equivalents of these dogmas and interrogate privileged systems of thought rather than accepting them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat claims of 'Truth' and 'Purity' with suspicion
rubrics_metrics.description: The unqualified use of 'true' and 'pure' in criticism is a warning sign; privileging a capital-'T' Truth imposes rigid, exclusionary standards on literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid classifying works as deficient because they don't meet an abstract True/Pure standard. Recognize that universality and shared community values can be valid without becoming dogmatic; critique 'purity' that excludes necessary human elements and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not exclude the reader from the critical equation
rubrics_metrics.description: A text's meaning and value depend on the interaction among author, text, and reader; excluding the reader (as purity doctrines often do) is a flawed approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for readers' responses and the role of readership communities in shaping meaning. Be wary of approaches that 'purify' the text by purging elements that enable reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge human emotion as intrinsic (reject 'emotion contaminates art')
rubrics_metrics.description: Human emotion cannot be removed from literary works; attempts to purge emotional content misunderstand how texts produce effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a critical stance treats emotion as incompatible with aesthetic pleasure, challenge it—even an absence of explicit emotion produces emotional responses. Avoid dehumanizing readings that privilege abstract formal properties over human relations and moral stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject monistic purity/realism; adopt pluralism
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than dismissing purity or realism wholesale, assess their insights pluralistically—each critical 'instrument' uncovers some truths and conceals others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Booth advocates converting monistic critical positions into pluralist practice: find value in opponents' views, temper universal claims, and be open to multiple legitimate interpretive lenses. Avoid superimposing rigid political or theoretical agendas that reduce textual complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze the author–text–reader relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: Booth's methodology centers on the dynamic relationship among author, text, and reader; analysis should divide these into workable parts and examine their interactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask how authorial choices (rhetoric, narration, style) invite particular reader responses and how the text mediates between them. Use neo-Aristotelian questioning about mechanics and coherence but acknowledge rhetoric is inevitable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the implied author via style, tone, and technique
rubrics_metrics.description: The implied author is a created version of the real author evidenced by the work's choices; Booth names three core components: style, tone, and technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'style' as the main source of insight into the author's norms; 'tone' as the implicit evaluation behind presentation; and 'technique' to cover signs of artistry. The implied author is what readers infer ethically and evaluatively from the text—focus on the work as evidence of authorial choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine narration as a rhetorical act (distance, navigator role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration is a rhetorical art that positions readers on a 'map' of meaning; distance and the narrator's handling guide readers' moral and evaluative judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how narrative distance directs sympathies and beliefs (e.g., Austen's navigational subtlety vs. Spillane's unethical narrator). Consider whether narrator and implied author converge or diverge, and whether the narrator functions as foil or authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate narrator reliability and ethical effects of narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrator reliability (or the lack of it) has moral consequences: impersonal or unreliable narration can produce confused or ethically suspect readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate whether narration leads readers toward a morally 'vicious marsh' or toward constructive understanding. Beware of unwarranted sympathy for morally repugnant narrators and ask how/why such narrators are made attractive or respected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and write ethically—seek good reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism and authorship involve ethical responsibility; Booth values 'good reasons' that balance ethics, emotions, and logic rather than pure scientism or radical scepticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the reader's moral habitus (values formed by community) and how that habitus shapes interpretation. Ethical reading means being attentive to the values a text promotes and the author's responsibility in shaping readers' perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not accept 'the Death of the Author' as total solution
rubrics_metrics.description: While rejecting critical monism, Booth objects to completely removing the author; instead use the concept of the implied author as a more knowable, text-based guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rather than treating the author as irrelevant or language as all, acknowledge that authorship (via implied author) plays a constitutive role in meaning-making. Use the implied author to avoid unverifiable talk about biographical author-intent while still recognizing authorial shaping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors must choose rhetoric—examine which rhetoric is employed
rubrics_metrics.description: The author cannot avoid rhetoric but can choose its kind; criticism should identify and evaluate the rhetorical choices authors make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on how rhetorical strategies (voice, irony, narrative framing) function to achieve aims; critique should consider whether those rhetorical choices responsibly guide readers or mislead them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider language without excluding human relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Language is central to reading, but privileging language as a separate system from human relations risks 'purifying' texts of moral and social content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance attention to semiotic/structural features with attention to how language connects to communal values and ethical meanings; decode language into meanings that fit value systems rather than treating signs as the whole object of study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be tentative and self-critical about textual selections and authorial tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Methodological claims should acknowledge the tentativeness of chosen examples and the voice of the critic or implied author; Booth admits earlier arrogance and recommends humility and pluralist correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending critical methods, disclose selection criteria and avoid an overconfident implied authorial voice. Make allowances for necessary extensions, clarifications, and modern examples to balance earlier emphases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the author's role in 'making' readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors shape readers' perceptions; criticism should judge whether authors 'make readers well' (expand perception) or merely wait for matching readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate authorial craft by whether it enlarges readers' vision and ethical capacities. Reward texts that move readers into new orders of perception rather than reinforcing narrow pre-existing norms.
